name: Limits on applications per institution in capacity programmes
what: Many capacity programmes cap what one institution may submit, so the institution chooses internally before the funder sees anything. Examples read in this sweep: MRI, two in Track 1, one in Track 2, one in Track 3 [1516](#cite:1516); E-CORE, E-RISE and FEC, one submission as lead [1520](#cite:1520) [1522](#cite:1522) [1524](#cite:1524); ART, one proposal for Track 1 or 2 and one per track for Tracks 3 to 5 [1528](#cite:1528); [S10](#term:s10) Seed Instrumentation, one application [1537](#cite:1537); C06, one application per institution [1542](#cite:1542); COBRE-D, one application and no active COBRE [grant](#term:grant) [1545](#cite:1545); IDeA-CTR, one active award per state [1552](#cite:1552); DOE [EPSCoR](#term:epscor), two lead submissions per programme area [1569](#cite:1569); NASA EPSCoR R3, three proposals per institution [1573](#cite:1573). DURIP states no limit [1563](#cite:1563).

name: NSF EPSCoR co-funding
what: [EPSCoR](#term:epscor) often co-funds proposals submitted to other [NSF](#term:nsf) programmes when the applicant is in an EPSCoR jurisdiction; the applicant does not apply for it separately [1518](#cite:1518). The EPSCoR report in the FY 2027 request shows $33.38 million of co-funding in FY 2025 [255](#cite:255).

name: NIH IDeA co-funding
what: NIGMS adds money to [R01](#term:r01), [R15](#term:r15) and MIRA R35 applications from investigators in [IDeA states](#term:idea-program) that an [NIH](#term:nih) institute did not select for funding: up to $350,000 in total costs for each of the first two years [1553](#cite:1553). It runs once a year; [nominations](#term:institutional-nomination) typically open in January or February and close in early April, and decisions typically come in June or July [1553](#cite:1553). All [PIs](#term:principal-investigator) and performance sites must be in IDeA-eligible states [1553](#cite:1553).

name: NSF EPSCoR renewal cost share
what: E-CORE and E-RISE prohibit voluntary committed [cost sharing](#term:cost-sharing) on the first award and require cost sharing of at least, and no more than, 20% of the amount requested on a [renewal](#term:renewal) [1520](#cite:1520) [1522](#cite:1522).

name: No indirect costs on NIH S10 and C06 awards
what: [S10](#term:s10) awards do not allow [indirect costs](#term:indirect-costs) [1536](#cite:1536) [1537](#cite:1537). The C06 notice lists F&A costs as [unallowable](#term:allowable-cost) [1542](#cite:1542). DURIP treats equipment costs as exempt from indirect costs [1563](#cite:1563).

name: NIH S10 major-user requirement
what: An [S10](#term:s10) application rests on named NIH-funded users of the instrument: at least three Major Users with active [NIH](#term:nih) research awards for the Shared Instrumentation [Grant](#term:grant), and at least two NIH-funded users, one from the applicant institution, for Seed Instrumentation Support [1536](#cite:1536) [1537](#cite:1537).

name: NIH C06 ten-year use requirement
what: A facility built or improved with a C06 award must be used for the biomedical research purposes for which it was built or improved for at least 10 years [1542](#cite:1542).

name: NIH CTSA budget tiers
what: The budget a CTSA hub may request is set by the institution's five-year average of [NIH](#term:nih) [direct costs](#term:direct-costs), in four tiers, from up to $2,600,000 to up to $6,500,000 as the fetch returned them [1559](#cite:1559).

name: DURIP is issued by three offices under three numbers
what: ONR, the Army [Research Office](#term:sponsored-programs-office) and AFOSR each post the same DURIP announcement under their own number, and the applicant submits to the office whose research the instrument serves [1563](#cite:1563) [1561](#cite:1561).

name: EPSCoR-type lists differ by agency
what: Six agencies keep lists of jurisdictions for capacity programmes and the lists are not the same. [NSF](#term:nsf) lists 28 jurisdictions and its list is frozen through FY 2027 [1517](#cite:1517). DOE and NASA follow the NSF list [1567](#cite:1567) [1574](#cite:1574). DEPSCoR lists 36 states and territories [1565](#cite:1565). USDA lists 19 states for FY 2026 plus the District of Columbia and insular areas [1576](#cite:1576). [NIH](#term:nih) lists 23 states and Puerto Rico for IDeA [1543](#cite:1543). A state can be on one list and off another: Alabama and Iowa, for example, are on the NSF, DOE, NASA and DEPSCoR lists and not on the NIH IDeA or USDA FY 2026 lists [1517](#cite:1517) [1567](#cite:1567) [1573](#cite:1573) [1565](#cite:1565) [1543](#cite:1543) [1576](#cite:1576).

name: Eligibility Matrix
what: The Department of Education's yearly set of programme lists, built from IPEDS data, showing which institutions meet each programme definition; the Department uses it to pre-determine eligibility [1595](#cite:1595) [1596](#cite:1596). Meeting a definition or holding a [grant](#term:grant) does not by itself make an institution eligible for new funding [1595](#cite:1595).

name: Individual development and cooperative arrangement development grants
what: [Title III](#term:title-iii-v-eligibility) Part A and Title V competitions offer two [grant](#term:grant) types: an individual development grant to one institution and a cooperative arrangement development grant to institutions working together, each with its own ceiling and application limit [1600](#cite:1600) [1644](#cite:1644).

name: Two-year wait-out period (34 CFR 607.9)
what: An institution whose Strengthening Institutions individual development [grant](#term:grant) has ended waits two years before it may receive another; in FY 2026 former grantees whose five-year grants ended on or before September 30, 2024 could apply for individual grants [1600](#cite:1600).

name: Endowment match under Title III and Title V
what: A grantee may put no more than 20 percent of an annual award into an endowment fund and matches that money with non-federal funds [1599](#cite:1599) [1617](#cite:1617). Apart from this the [Title III](#term:title-iii-v-eligibility) Part A and Title V notices read required no [cost sharing](#term:cost-sharing) [1600](#cite:1600) [1642](#cite:1642).

name: Mandatory funding under Title III Part F
what: Section 371 of the Higher Education Act appropriates $255,000,000 a year directly, outside the annual [appropriations](#term:appropriations-act) bill, and divides it among seven institution classes [1661](#cite:1661). The Department of Education said in 2025 that such mandatory funds cannot be reprogrammed [1594](#cite:1594).

name: NSF opportunity pages marked "waiting for new publication" or "archived"
what: An [NSF](#term:nsf) opportunity page labelled as waiting for a new publication lists the previous [solicitation](#term:program-solicitation) and no due dates; an archived page is a past solicitation that is no longer active [1611](#cite:1611) [1612](#cite:1612) [882](#cite:882) [1660](#cite:1660).

name: Community Project Funding and Congressionally Directed Spending (the earmark process)
what: Congress may name a specific recipient, project and amount in an [appropriations act](#term:appropriations-act); the House calls this [Community Project Funding](#term:community-project-funding) and the Senate Congressionally Directed Spending [1667](#cite:1667) [1674](#cite:1674). An organisation cannot apply to either committee: it asks its House Member or a Senator, on that office's own deadline, and the office decides whether to submit the request to the committee [1667](#cite:1667) [1674](#cite:1674). Recipients may be state, local or tribal governments and certain eligible non-profits; for-profit entities are excluded in both chambers [1667](#cite:1667) [1675](#cite:1675). Projects are listed in a table in the joint explanatory statement of the enacted act, and the agency then awards only to the named recipient [1679](#cite:1679) [1686](#cite:1686). Congress designated no such funds in FY 2025: the full-year [continuing resolution](#term:continuing-resolution) gave prior-year project language no legal effect [1680](#cite:1680) [1755](#cite:1755). FY2026 projects were enacted in four laws signed between November 12, 2025 and April 30, 2026 [1677](#cite:1677). FY27 requests were due to the committees between March 13 and May 7, 2026; on the sweep date no FY2027 act had been enacted and continuing appropriations ran through December 11, 2026 [1668](#cite:1668) [1675](#cite:1675) [61](#cite:61).

name: Rules on earmark requests (caps, certification, posting, audit)
what: House, FY27: at most 20 requests per Member across bills; total [Community Project Funding](#term:community-project-funding) at most one half of one percent of discretionary spending; no for-profit recipients; no memorials, museums or commemoratives; a written federal nexus statement and evidence of community support for each request; the Member certifies that the Member and immediate family have no financial interest and posts every request online in a searchable format [1667](#cite:1667). Senate, FY27: funding for these items at most one percent of discretionary spending; for-profit entities ineligible; a per-Senator limit set by each subcommittee; the Senator certifies no financial interest and publishes requests and the certification on the Senator's website [1675](#cite:1675) [1674](#cite:1674). In both chambers the Government Accountability Office audits a sample of enacted projects [1667](#cite:1667) [1675](#cite:1675).

name: Accounts that take earmark requests, FY2027
what: A request must fit one of the accounts a subcommittee has opened [1669](#cite:1669). House, FY27: Community Facilities, Distance Learning and Telemedicine, ARS Buildings and Facilities and two other Agriculture accounts; NIST Scientific and Technical Research, NOAA Coastal Zone Management, NASA Safety, Security and Mission Services and two Justice accounts; FEMA Emergency Operations Centers and Pre-Disaster Mitigation; EPA water revolving funds; [HRSA](#term:hrsa) only in Labor-HHS-Education; HUD Economic Development Initiatives and five Transportation accounts; military construction; Army Corps and Reclamation accounts [1669](#cite:1669). The House takes no requests in Defense, Financial Services, Legislative Branch or National Security and State [1668](#cite:1668). Senate, FY27: the list is wider and adds NIST Construction of Research Facilities, the Small Business Administration, the National Historical Publications and Records Commission, National Park Service Historic Preservation Fund Projects, and, in Labor-HHS-Education, the Employment and Training Administration, [SAMHSA](#term:samhsa), the Administration for Children and Families, the Administration for Community Living and two Education accounts [1675](#cite:1675). The Senate takes no requests in Defense, Legislative Branch or State-Foreign Operations [1675](#cite:1675).

name: The agency application that follows an earmark
what: Being named in the act does not release the money: the named recipient still applies to the agency, which checks the project against the congressional direction and its own rules [1686](#cite:1686) [1672](#cite:1672). For FY2026, HUD emailed [grant](#term:grant) packages from late April 2026, [HRSA](#term:hrsa) set a June 1, 2026 deadline under two closed notices, [SAMHSA](#term:samhsa) posted a closed announcement on June 12, 2026, and the Department of Labor issued instructions on August 21, 2026 with a window to January 31, 2027 [1685](#cite:1685) [1687](#cite:1687) [1688](#cite:1688) [1690](#cite:1690). GAO estimated that 61 percent of the $39 billion designated for FY2022 to FY2024 had been obligated and about 16 percent paid out by the end of FY 2024, and that an estimated 60 percent of recipients reported at least one challenge in carrying out their project [1681](#cite:1681).

name: Environmental review before funds are committed (capital projects)
what: For a HUD Economic Development Initiative project an environmental review must be completed before HUD funds or non-HUD funds are committed to or spent on the project, under 24 [CFR](#term:cfr) Part 50 or 58 [1673](#cite:1673) [1685](#cite:1685). [HRSA](#term:hrsa) construction projects file an Environmental Information Document checklist with the application [1687](#cite:1687).

name: Notice of Federal Interest (HRSA capital awards)
what: A document that [HRSA](#term:hrsa) construction awards require to be filed for the property where it applies; HRSA publishes a sample [1687](#cite:1687) [1737](#cite:1737).

name: Capacity money awarded to an intermediary that serves local organisations
what: Several capacity programmes are awarded to a national or regional body and reach a local organisation only as training, technical assistance or a [subgrant](#term:subaward) from that body [1712](#cite:1712) [1704](#cite:1704). HUD Section 4 goes to three named national non-profits and Rural Capacity Building to national non-profits [1712](#cite:1712) [1714](#cite:1714). Paul Bruhn primes may not fund their own properties [1704](#cite:1704). State Historical Records Advisory Boards may regrant to archives [700](#cite:700). Renew America's Nonprofits made subawards of up to $200,000 through prime recipients [1748](#cite:1748). Technical-assistance centre awards at HUD, [HRSA](#term:hrsa), [SAMHSA](#term:samhsa) and Justice pay the winner to assist others, not to build its own capacity [1715](#cite:1715) [1741](#cite:1741) [1746](#cite:1746) [1743](#cite:1743).

name: Grant, cooperative agreement and procurement contract
what: Federal law gives an agency three instruments for giving money to an outside body, and the choice follows from the purpose of the transaction [1851](#cite:1851). A grant agreement and a [cooperative agreement](#term:cooperative-agreement) both transfer something of value to carry out a public purpose that a law authorises; a [procurement contract](#term:procurement-contract) buys property or services for the Government's own direct benefit or use [1851](#cite:1851). The difference between a grant and a cooperative agreement is whether substantial involvement is expected between the agency and the recipient while the work is carried out [1851](#cite:1851).
rule: Under 31 U.S.C. 6304 an agency uses a grant agreement when the principal purpose is to transfer a thing of value for a public purpose of support or stimulation and substantial involvement is not expected; under 31 U.S.C. 6305 it uses a cooperative agreement on the same test when substantial involvement is expected; under 31 U.S.C. 6303 it uses a procurement contract when the principal purpose is to acquire property or services for the direct benefit or use of the Government [1851](#cite:1851). [2 CFR 200](#term:uniform-guidance).201 requires the agency or [pass-through entity](#term:pass-through-entity) to decide on the instrument under these sections [1807](#cite:1807). 2 CFR 200.1 defines both instruments in the same terms and adds that a pass-through entity may also be the substantially involved party in a cooperative agreement [1799](#cite:1799). The statute does not define "substantial involvement"; Appendix I to Part 200 requires a notice for a cooperative agreement to describe the substantial involvement the agency expects [1848](#cite:1848). 31 U.S.C. 6307 lets the Director of OMB issue interpretative guidelines and exempt a transaction or programme [1851](#cite:1851).

name: Assistance Listings
what: The [Assistance Listings](#term:assistance-listing) are the public catalogue of federal assistance programmes, kept by the General Services Administration at [SAM.gov](#term:sam-gov) [1799](#cite:1799) [1808](#cite:1808). Each programme has a listing and a number, and that number appears in the funding notice and in the award document [1800](#cite:1800) [1810](#cite:1810). The [Grants.gov](#term:grants-gov) glossary calls the listings the authoritative source of information about federal programmes that provide [grants](#term:grant), loans, scholarships, insurance and other assistance [1880](#cite:1880).
rule: [2 CFR 200](#term:uniform-guidance).203 requires each agency to keep an accurate list of its programmes in the Assistance Listings and to assign a listing before making awards, except in exigent circumstances [1808](#cite:1808). A listing gives the programme's purpose and goals, whether its awards are discretionary or non-discretionary, the projected funds, the source of funds, the general eligibility requirements and whether [single audit](#term:single-audit) requirements apply [1808](#cite:1808).
applies_to: Every [federal financial assistance](#term:financial-assistance) programme [1808](#cite:1808). A [pass-through entity](#term:pass-through-entity) must give the Assistance Listings title and number to each [subrecipient](#term:subrecipient) [1823](#cite:1823).

name: Discretionary, mandatory, formula and block awards
what: Federal awards divide by how the recipient and the amount are chosen [1880](#cite:1880). For a [discretionary grant](#term:discretionary-grant) the agency may select the recipient from among all eligible applicants, may decide whether to make an award on the content of an application, and decides the amount [1880](#cite:1880). For a [mandatory grant](#term:formula-grant) the authorising statute requires an award to each eligible entity in the amount or by the formula the statute sets, and a formula grant is an allocation to states, territories or local governments by a distribution formula in the law or regulations [1880](#cite:1880).
rule: [2 CFR 200](#term:uniform-guidance).1 defines a discretionary award as one in which the agency, under statutory authority to exercise judgment, selects the recipient or the amount through a competitive process or on the merit of proposals, and a non-discretionary award as one made to specific recipients under statutory, eligibility and compliance requirements such that the agency cannot exercise judgment [1894](#cite:1894). Each [Assistance Listing](#term:assistance-listing) states whether a programme's awards are discretionary or non-discretionary [1808](#cite:1808). The notice rules in 2 CFR 200.204 apply to discretionary funding opportunities [1800](#cite:1800). 2 CFR 200.101(e) takes [block grants](#term:block-grant) authorised by the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1981, and certain other listed programmes, out of subparts C, D and E except for specified provisions, and 200.101(f) takes listed entitlement programmes, among them TANF, Medicaid and CHIP, out of subpart C [1805](#cite:1805). [Executive Order 14332](#term:executive-order-14332) applies to discretionary grants only, and takes its definition from 2 CFR 200.1 [246](#cite:246). The [Grants.gov](#term:grants-gov) glossary read on 2026-10-04 has no entry for "block grant" [1880](#cite:1880).
applies_to: All [federal financial assistance](#term:financial-assistance); the distinction decides whether an organisation competes with a federal agency or applies to a state or local recipient [1880](#cite:1880) [1805](#cite:1805). The pack's record pass-through-subaward describes the second route [1823](#cite:1823).

pending_changes.text: [OMB](#term:omb)'s [proposed rule](#term:proposed-rule) would require every federal funding opportunity to be posted on [Grants.gov](#term:grants-gov), with an exception an agency head may approve where public announcement poses a national security risk, and would revise Appendix I [1803](#cite:1803) [1458](#cite:1458).
[Executive Order 14332](#term:executive-order-14332) requires a senior appointee to review new funding opportunity announcements before they issue [246](#cite:246).

Read in the [Federal Register](#term:federal-register) text of OMB's proposal: 200.204 would require agencies to announce funding opportunities publicly for all [discretionary awards](#term:discretionary-grant), not only those openly competed, with opportunities posted for no less than 30 days unless exigent circumstances exist; 200.205 would require the [merit review process](#term:merit-review), including a pre-issuance review, to be described in the notice; 200.111 would require announcements and applications to be in English and in U.S. dollars [2092](#cite:2092) [2093](#cite:2093).

name: Notice of funding opportunity: required content and time open
what: A [notice of funding opportunity](#term:nofo) is the formal announcement that federal funding is available through a [financial assistance](#term:financial-assistance) programme [1799](#cite:1799). The [Uniform Guidance](#term:uniform-guidance) fixes what a notice must contain, in what order, and how long it is expected to stay open [1800](#cite:1800) [1848](#cite:1848). A summary of each notice is displayed on Grants.gov ahead of the full text [1800](#cite:1800).
rule: 2 CFR 200.204(a) lists the summary items: agency name, opportunity title, announcement type, [funding opportunity number](#term:opportunity-number), [Assistance Listing number](#term:assistance-listing), funding details, key dates, an executive summary and agency contact information [1800](#cite:1800). 2 CFR 200.204(b) sets a standard of at least 60 calendar days open for application, allows a shorter period, and states that no opportunity is to be open for fewer than 30 calendar days unless the agency determines that exigent circumstances justify it; the paragraph is worded as an expectation ("should"), not as a requirement [1800](#cite:1800). Appendix I sets nine sections for the full text: Basic Information; Eligibility; Program Description; Application Contents and Format; Submission Requirements and Deadlines; Application Review Information; Award Notices; Post-Award Requirements and Administration; and Other Information, which is optional [1848](#cite:1848). The notice must state whether [cost sharing](#term:cost-sharing) is required, and say so if it is not; must list every type of eligible applicant; must describe each review criterion and its relative weight where weights differ; must describe the [risk review](#term:risk-review) under 200.206; and must state the agency's policies on [indirect cost](#term:indirect-costs) rate reimbursement [1848](#cite:1848) [1802](#cite:1802). The notice must be written in plain language [1848](#cite:1848). The [eCFR](#term:cfr)'s version record for part 200, read on 2026-10-04, lists no issue of 200.204 after the amendment dated October 1, 2024 [2103](#cite:2103).

name: The Uniform Guidance (2 CFR part 200)
what: The [Uniform Guidance](#term:uniform-guidance) is the government-wide set of administrative requirements, [cost principles](#term:cost-principles) and audit requirements for federal awards, issued by the Office of Management and Budget as 2 CFR part 200 [1799](#cite:1799) [1805](#cite:1805). The text in force on 2026-10-04 is the revision published April 22, 2024 at 89 FR 30046, effective October 1, 2024 [1883](#cite:1883) [1801](#cite:1801). A proposed replacement was published May 29, 2026 and, under section 157 of Public Law 119-103, may not be issued or take effect through December 11, 2026 [1458](#cite:1458) [1480](#cite:1480).
rule: Subpart A holds definitions and subpart B general provisions; both apply to all federal financial assistance [1805](#cite:1805). Subparts C (pre-award) and D (post-award) apply to [grants](#term:grant) and [cooperative agreements](#term:cooperative-agreement); subpart E (cost principles) applies to them except fixed amount awards and certain other cases; subpart F (audit) applies to grants and cooperative agreements, cost-type contracts and other assistance under the [Single Audit](#term:single-audit) Act [1805](#cite:1805). The part binds federal agencies that make awards and, through the award terms, recipients and [subrecipients](#term:subrecipient); the terms flow down to [subawards](#term:subaward) unless a section or the award says otherwise [1805](#cite:1805). A federal statute or regulation governs where it conflicts with the part [1805](#cite:1805). An agency may apply subparts A to E to for-profit organisations, foreign public entities and foreign organisations where its regulations or a statute allow [1805](#cite:1805). Under 200.110 the standards take effect once implemented by federal agencies or when an amendment becomes final [1806](#cite:1806). Each agency adopts the part in its own chapter of 2 [CFR](#term:cfr); [HHS](#term:hhs), for example, adopts it at 2 CFR 300.106 with additions, and applied it from October 1, 2025 in place of 45 CFR part 75 [1884](#cite:1884) [528](#cite:528) [65](#cite:65). In the text "must" marks a requirement and "should" or "may" a discretionary matter [1805](#cite:1805). Checked on 2026-10-04: the eCFR showed title 2 as up to date as of 10/01/2026 and last amended 8/17/2026 [2102](#cite:2102) [1940](#cite:1940). The eCFR's version record for part 200 gives October 1, 2024 as the latest amendment date of the part and lists four later issues, each marked not substantive: section 200.1, section 200.405, Appendix VII and Appendix XII [2103](#cite:2103). The source note of 200.1 reads 89 FR 30136, April 22, 2024, as amended at 89 FR 79732, October 1, 2024 [2102](#cite:2102). The [Federal Register](#term:federal-register) index holds two rule documents citing 2 CFR part 200 since April 23, 2024, both from 2024, one of them OMB's corrections of October 1, 2024, and none dated 2025 or 2026 [2094](#cite:2094). Six rule documents citing title 2 were published from January 1, 2025 to 2026-10-04, all in agency chapters of Subtitle B; the one effective August 17, 2026 is the Department of Energy's rule adding subpart C to 2 CFR part 910 [2095](#cite:2095) [2096](#cite:2096).

variants.what: Before making an award a federal agency reviews the risk an applicant poses [2023](#cite:2023).
variants.rule: [2 CFR 200](#term:uniform-guidance).206: the agency reviews eligibility and financial integrity information in governmentwide databases and, for awards above the simplified acquisition threshold, the responsibility and qualification records in the non-public segment of [SAM.gov](#term:sam-gov) [2023](#cite:2023). The section lists what an agency is to consider: financial stability, the quality of management systems and the ability to meet management standards, history of performance on federal awards, audit reports and findings, and the ability to implement requirements [2023](#cite:2023). The agency may adjust its assessment during the award and change the award's terms [2023](#cite:2023).
variants.applies_to: All applicants for [federal financial assistance](#term:financial-assistance) [2023](#cite:2023). [HHS](#term:hhs) describes its review as a cost analysis of the budget, an assessment of management systems, a final review of eligibility and a check of compliance with public policy requirements [528](#cite:528). [NSF](#term:nsf) asks a prospective new awardee for audited financial statements from the previous two years, income statements, statements of cash flows, federal tax returns and a completed Financial Management System Questionnaire [2072](#cite:2072). The Office of Justice Programs has every applicant other than an individual complete a Financial Management and System of Internal Controls Questionnaire in [JustGrants](#term:justgrants), which asks whether any federal agency has designated the applicant high risk; for awards exceeding $250,000 it also reviews the applicant's records in SAM.gov [619](#cite:619).

name: Pre-award risk review and specific conditions
what: Before it makes an award a federal agency reviews the risk the applicant poses [1809](#cite:1809). The review can end in an award with extra conditions attached [1886](#cite:1886). The criteria the agency uses must be described in the funding announcement [1809](#cite:1809).
rule: Under 2 CFR 200.206(a) the agency checks eligibility and financial integrity information in OMB-designated databases, and reviews the non-public segment of SAM.gov where the Federal share is expected to exceed the simplified acquisition threshold over the [period of performance](#term:budget-period) [1809](#cite:1809). Under 200.206(b) the agency keeps written procedures for a [risk assessment](#term:risk-review), which may consider financial stability, management systems and standards, history of performance, audit reports and findings, and the ability to implement requirements effectively [1809](#cite:1809). The assessment may be changed at any time during the period of performance [1809](#cite:1809). Under 200.206(d) awards, [subawards](#term:subaward) and contracts with debarred, suspended or excluded parties are restricted under 2 [CFR](#term:cfr) part 180 [1809](#cite:1809). Under 200.208 the agency or [pass-through entity](#term:pass-through-entity) may impose specific conditions: payment by reimbursement instead of advance, withholding authority to proceed to the next phase, more detailed financial reports, additional monitoring, required technical or management assistance, or additional prior approvals [1886](#cite:1886). The agency must tell the recipient the nature of the condition, the reason, the action needed, the time allowed and how to ask for reconsideration, and must remove the condition promptly once it is satisfied [1886](#cite:1886).
applies_to: Every applicant for a federal [grant](#term:grant) or [cooperative agreement](#term:cooperative-agreement); a pass-through entity runs a parallel review of each [subrecipient](#term:subrecipient) under 200.332 [1809](#cite:1809) [1823](#cite:1823).

variants.what: A recipient's accounting system has to be able to do seven things listed in the [Uniform Guidance](#term:uniform-guidance); an agency checks an applicant's system against them before a first award [2068](#cite:2068) [528](#cite:528).
variants.rule: 2 CFR 200.302(b): the system identifies all federal awards received and expended; gives accurate, current and complete disclosure of the financial results of each award; keeps records that identify the amount, source and expenditure of federal funds; keeps effective control over and accountability for all funds, property and assets; compares expenditures with budget amounts for each award; and has written procedures for payments and for determining the allowability of costs [2068](#cite:2068).

name: Financial management standards for recipients
what: A recipient's accounting system has to be able to show, award by award, what federal money came in and how it was spent [1811](#cite:1811). The standard is in 2 CFR 200.302, and the payment rules that go with it are in 200.305 [1811](#cite:1811) [1813](#cite:1813).
rule: 2 CFR 200.302(b) requires a system that provides: identification of every federal award received and expended and its programme; accurate, current and complete disclosure of financial results; records that identify the amount, source and expenditure of federal funds; effective control over and accountability for all funds, property and assets; comparison of expenditures with budget amounts; written procedures to implement the payment rules in 200.305; and written procedures for determining the allowability of costs [1811](#cite:1811). States account for awards under their own laws and procedures [1811](#cite:1811). Under 200.305 advance payments are limited to the minimum amounts needed and timed to actual, immediate cash requirements; where payment is by reimbursement the agency or pass-through entity pays within 30 calendar days of receiving the request [1813](#cite:1813). Advances are kept in interest-bearing accounts unless the recipient receives less than $250,000 in federal funding a year or the account would not be expected to earn more than $500 a year, and up to $500 a year of interest may be kept for administrative expenses [1813](#cite:1813). name: Internal controls
what: Internal controls are the processes that give reasonable assurance that an award is managed in compliance with federal statutes, regulations and the award terms [1812](#cite:1812). [2 CFR 200](#term:uniform-guidance).303 makes them a duty of every recipient and [subrecipient](#term:subrecipient) [1812](#cite:1812).
rule: 2 CFR 200.303 requires a recipient or subrecipient to establish, document and maintain effective internal control over the award; to comply with the Constitution, federal statutes, regulations and the award terms; to evaluate and monitor its own compliance; to take prompt action when noncompliance is identified; and to take reasonable cybersecurity and other measures to safeguard information, including protected personally identifiable information [1812](#cite:1812). The [eCFR](#term:cfr)'s version record for part 200, read on 2026-10-04, gives October 1, 2024 as the latest amendment date of the part; the only later issues are of 200.1, 200.405, Appendix VII and Appendix XII, each marked not substantive [2103](#cite:2103).

name: Cost sharing and matching under the Uniform Guidance
what: [Cost sharing](#term:cost-sharing), also called matching, is the part of project cost not paid by federal funds [1880](#cite:1880). Whether a programme requires it is stated in the funding notice, which must also say so when it is not required [1848](#cite:1848). For research [grants](#term:grant) the [Uniform Guidance](#term:uniform-guidance) says voluntary committed cost sharing is not expected [1814](#cite:1814).
rule: Under 2 CFR 200.306(a) an agency may not use voluntary committed cost sharing as a factor in [merit review](#term:merit-review) of research proposals unless a statute or agency regulation authorises it and the notice says so [1814](#cite:1814). Under 200.306(b) a contribution counts as cost sharing only if it is verifiable in the recipient's records, is not counted for any other federal award, is necessary and reasonable, is allowable under subpart E, is not paid by the Federal Government under another award unless a statute allows it, is in the approved budget when the agency requires, and conforms to the rest of the part [1814](#cite:1814). Paragraphs (c) to (k) cover unrecovered [indirect costs](#term:indirect-costs) and the valuation and documentation of donated services, property and volunteer time [1814](#cite:1814). A fixed amount award may not be used in a programme that requires cost sharing [1807](#cite:1807). A change in approved cost sharing needs [prior approval](#term:prior-approval) [1815](#cite:1815). The [eCFR](#term:cfr) page for 200.306 returned rate-limit errors twice on 2026-10-04 and was not re-read there; the eCFR's version record for part 200 gives October 1, 2024 as the latest amendment date of the part and lists no later issue of 200.306 [2103](#cite:2103).
applies_to: Any award whose statute, regulation or notice requires a non-federal share; the pack records programme-specific rules under ids such as nsf-cost-sharing, nifa-matching and nea-one-to-one-cost-share [1814](#cite:1814).

name: Period of performance, budget period and pre-award costs
what: The [period of performance](#term:budget-period) is the time between the start and end date of an award, and it may contain one or more budget periods [1799](#cite:1799). A budget period is the funded portion during which the recipient is authorised to incur financial obligations [1799](#cite:1799). Both pairs of dates are printed in the award document [1810](#cite:1810). Costs incurred before the start date are pre-award costs and are allowable only on the terms below [1843](#cite:1843).
rule: Under [2 CFR 200](#term:uniform-guidance).403(h) costs must be incurred during the approved budget period, except administrative [closeout](#term:closeout) costs, which may be incurred until the due date of the final reports [1831](#cite:1831). Under 200.458 pre-award costs are those incurred before the start date directly pursuant to the negotiation and in anticipation of the award, where necessary for efficient and timely performance; they are allowable only to the extent they would have been allowable after the start date and only with the agency's written approval [1843](#cite:1843). Under 200.308 an agency may waive that approval so that a recipient may incur project costs up to 90 calendar days before the award date, may let a recipient start a one-time extension of the period of performance of up to 12 months on notice at least 10 calendar days before the period ends, and may let unobligated balances be carried forward to later budget periods [1815](#cite:1815). Under 200.309 an extension moves the end date, a [termination](#term:termination) ends the period on its effective date, and a [renewal](#term:renewal) award begins a new and distinct period of performance [1816](#cite:1816). A funding notice must tell applicants that work begun before the award is at the applicant's own risk [1848](#cite:1848). The [eCFR](#term:cfr)'s version record for part 200, read on 2026-10-04, gives October 1, 2024 as the latest amendment date of the part; the only later issues are of 200.1, 200.405, Appendix VII and Appendix XII, each marked not substantive [2103](#cite:2103). The eCFR text of 200.308 current to 10/01/2026 has the same 90-day pre-award period and the same one-time extension of up to 12 months [2118](#cite:2118).

name: Prior approval requirements
what: Some changes to a funded project, and some kinds of cost, need the agency's written approval before the recipient acts [1815](#cite:1815) [1834](#cite:1834). The [Uniform Guidance](#term:uniform-guidance) lists them in two places: 200.308 for changes to the budget and programme, and 200.407 for cost items [1815](#cite:1815) [1834](#cite:1834).
rule: 2 CFR 200.308 requires [prior approval](#term:prior-approval) for a change in scope or objective; a change in key personnel; disengagement of the [project director](#term:principal-investigator) for more than three months or a 25 percent reduction in time; costs that need approval under subpart E; transfer of [participant support costs](#term:participant-support-costs) to other categories; subawarding work not in the approved application; changes in approved [cost sharing](#term:cost-sharing); a need for additional federal funds; and a [no-cost extension](#term:no-cost-extension) beyond the one-time extension [1815](#cite:1815). An agency may also restrict transfers among cost categories where the Federal share exceeds the simplified acquisition threshold and the cumulative transfer exceeds or is expected to exceed 10 percent of the total budget [1815](#cite:1815). The agency should notify the recipient within 30 days of receipt whether a requested revision is approved; the section says should, not must [1815](#cite:1815). 2 CFR 200.407 lists sixteen sections where prior written approval is a condition of allowability, among them 200.306 cost sharing, 200.307 program income, 200.333 fixed amount [subawards](#term:subaward), 200.430(h) compensation, 200.431 fringe benefits, 200.439 equipment, 200.455 organization costs, 200.458 pre-award costs and 200.475 travel [1834](#cite:1834). For [indirect costs](#term:indirect-costs) the approval comes from the [cognizant agency for indirect costs](#term:cognizant-agency) [1834](#cite:1834). Absence of prior approval does not by itself make a cost unreasonable or unallocable unless one of the listed sections requires it [1834](#cite:1834). name: Procurement by recipients (2 CFR 200.317 to 200.327)
what: When a recipient spends award money on goods or services it follows the procurement standards in the [Uniform Guidance](#term:uniform-guidance), not the Federal Acquisition Regulation [1817](#cite:1817). The standards scale with the size of the purchase: micro-purchases, simplified acquisitions, and formal sealed bids or proposals [1819](#cite:1819). This record gives the outline only [1818](#cite:1818).
rule: A State or Indian Tribe follows the procedures it uses for its own funds; every other recipient and [subrecipient](#term:subrecipient), including a subrecipient of a State, follows 200.318 to 200.327 [1817](#cite:1817). Under 200.318 a recipient keeps documented procurement procedures, oversees its contractors, keeps written standards of conduct on conflicts of interest, avoids unnecessary or duplicative purchases, awards only to responsible contractors and keeps records that detail the history of each procurement [1818](#cite:1818). Under 200.320 a micro-purchase may be made without competitive quotations if the price is considered reasonable and that is documented; a simplified acquisition needs price or rate quotations from an adequate number of qualified sources; above the simplified acquisition threshold sealed bids or competitive proposals are used [1819](#cite:1819). The micro-purchase and simplified acquisition thresholds are those set by the Federal Acquisition Regulation at 48 [CFR](#term:cfr) part 2, subpart 2.1 [1799](#cite:1799). FAR 2.101, as shown on Acquisition.gov with an effective date of March 13, 2026, sets the micro-purchase threshold at $15,000, with other amounts for construction, services and emergencies; the simplified acquisition threshold figure was not reached in this sweep [1890]. A recipient may self-certify a micro-purchase threshold of up to $50,000 if it is a low-risk auditee, has an annual internal institutional [risk assessment](#term:risk-review), or, for a public institution, State law is consistent with it; a higher threshold needs approval from the [cognizant agency for indirect costs](#term:cognizant-agency) [1819](#cite:1819). Noncompetitive procurement is allowed in five cases: a micro-purchase; a single source; public exigency or emergency; written approval from the agency or [pass-through entity](#term:pass-through-entity); or inadequate competition after soliciting several sources [1819](#cite:1819). Equipment is tangible personal property with a useful life of more than one year and a unit cost at or above the lesser of the recipient's own capitalisation level or $10,000 [1799]. The eCFR text of 200.320 current to 10/01/2026 has the same $50,000 ceiling for a self-certified micro-purchase threshold, with approval by the cognizant agency for indirect costs above it [2091](#cite:2091). In the eCFR text of 200.1 the definitions of micro-purchase threshold and simplified acquisition threshold print no dollar figure: they refer to 200.320 and to the amounts set in the FAR at 48 CFR part 2, subpart 2.1, and the recipient or subrecipient sets a simplified acquisition threshold no higher than the FAR value [2102](#cite:2102).

name: Financial and performance reporting, and record retention
what: A recipient reports to the agency on money and on progress at intervals the award sets, and keeps its records for a fixed time after the last report [1820](#cite:1820) [1821](#cite:1821) [1825](#cite:1825). The [Uniform Guidance](#term:uniform-guidance) sets the outer limits on frequency and the due dates [1820](#cite:1820).
rule: Under 2 CFR 200.328 financial reports use OMB-approved data elements such as the [Federal Financial Report (SF-425)](#term:federal-financial-report), and are collected no less than annually and no more often than quarterly [1820](#cite:1820). Under 200.329 performance reports follow the same limits unless specific conditions apply; they compare accomplishments with objectives, explain why goals were not met, and explain cost overruns [1821](#cite:1821). For both kinds, an annual report is due no later than 90 calendar days after the reporting period, a quarterly or semiannual report no later than 30 calendar days after, and the final report no later than 120 calendar days after the [period of performance](#term:budget-period), or 90 calendar days for a [subrecipient](#term:subrecipient) [1820](#cite:1820) [1821](#cite:1821). A recipient must tell the agency of a significant development between reports [1821](#cite:1821). Under 200.334 records are kept for three years from the date the final financial report is submitted [1825](#cite:1825). The period runs longer while litigation, a claim or an audit finding is unresolved, or when the agency extends it in writing; property and equipment records are kept for three years after final disposition [1825](#cite:1825). Financial reports and payment requests carry a signed certification under 200.415 [1885](#cite:1885). name: Closeout
what: [Closeout](#term:closeout) is the process by which the agency or [pass-through entity](#term:pass-through-entity) determines that the administrative work of an award is complete [1830](#cite:1830). It follows the end of the [period of performance](#term:budget-period), including an end brought about by [termination](#term:termination) [1801](#cite:1801) [1816](#cite:1816).
rule: Under [2 CFR 200](#term:uniform-guidance).344 a recipient must submit all financial, performance and other reports, and liquidate all financial obligations, no later than 120 calendar days after the end of the period of performance; a [subrecipient](#term:subrecipient) has 90 calendar days [1830](#cite:1830). Funds paid and not authorised to be retained must be refunded promptly [1830](#cite:1830). The agency must make every effort to complete closeout actions no later than one year after the end of the period of performance [1830](#cite:1830). Where a recipient does not comply, the agency must report the material failure in [SAM.gov](#term:sam-gov) [1830](#cite:1830). Administrative closeout costs may be incurred until the due date of the final reports [1831](#cite:1831). After a termination both parties remain responsible for closeout under 200.344 and for later adjustments under 200.345 [1801](#cite:1801). The [eCFR](#term:cfr) page for 200.344 returned server errors twice on 2026-10-04 and was not re-read there; the eCFR's version record for part 200 gives October 1, 2024 as the latest amendment date of the part and lists no later issue of 200.344 [2103](#cite:2103).

name: Cost principles: allowable, reasonable, allocable
what: The [cost principles](#term:cost-principles) in subpart E of the [Uniform Guidance](#term:uniform-guidance) decide what an award may pay for [1831](#cite:1831). A cost charged to an award has to be allowable, and to be allowable it has to be reasonable and allocable, among other tests [1831](#cite:1831). Subpart E then gives rules for named items of cost, of which a few are outlined here [1834](#cite:1834).
rule: Under 2 CFR 200.403 a cost must be necessary and reasonable and allocable to the award; conform to limits in the principles or the award; be consistent with policies the organisation applies to its non-federal activities; be treated consistently as direct or indirect; follow generally accepted accounting principles; not be used as [cost sharing](#term:cost-sharing) for another federal programme; be adequately documented; and be incurred in the approved [budget period](#term:budget-period) [1831](#cite:1831). Under 200.404 a cost is reasonable if it does not exceed what a prudent person would incur in the circumstances when the decision was made [1832](#cite:1832). Under 200.405 a cost is allocable to an award according to the relative benefits received, and a cost allocable to one federal award may not be moved to another to overcome a funding shortfall [1833](#cite:1833). Under 200.413 [direct costs](#term:direct-costs) are those identified specifically with a final cost objective such as an award; salaries of administrative and clerical staff may be charged directly only if the services are integral to the award, the individuals can be specifically identified with it, and the costs are not also recovered as [indirect costs](#term:indirect-costs) [1835](#cite:1835). Selected items: compensation (200.430) is allowable when reasonable, consistent with the organisation's policy and supported by records that reflect the work performed, and budget estimates alone do not qualify as support [1837](#cite:1837); alcoholic beverages are unallowable (200.423) [1836](#cite:1836); entertainment is unallowable unless it has a specific and direct programmatic purpose and is in the award (200.438) [1838](#cite:1838); equipment and other capital expenditures are unallowable as indirect costs, and special purpose equipment with a unit cost of $10,000 or more needs prior written approval (200.439) [1839](#cite:1839); organised fundraising is unallowable (200.442) [1840](#cite:1840); lobbying costs are unallowable, with further restrictions for non-profits and [institutions of higher education](#term:institution-of-higher-education) (200.450) [1841](#cite:1841); [participant support costs](#term:participant-support-costs) are allowable and are left out of the indirect cost base (200.456, 200.1) [1842](#cite:1842) [1799](#cite:1799); travel is allowable within the organisation's written policy, and airfare above the least expensive unrestricted class is unallowable with five exceptions (200.475) [1844](#cite:1844). name: Remedies for noncompliance
what: When a recipient fails to comply with the Constitution, a federal statute or regulation, or the award terms, the agency or [pass-through entity](#term:pass-through-entity) has a graded set of remedies short of and including termination [1826](#cite:1826). The first step is specific conditions under 200.208 [1826](#cite:1826) [1886](#cite:1886).
rule: Under [2 CFR 200](#term:uniform-guidance).339 the agency or pass-through entity may impose specific conditions, and where noncompliance cannot be remedied that way it may: temporarily withhold payments until corrective action is taken; disallow costs for all or part of the activity; suspend or terminate the award in part or in its entirety; initiate suspension or debarment proceedings under 2 [CFR](#term:cfr) part 180; withhold further federal funds, whether new awards or [continuation](#term:continuation) funding, for the project or programme; or pursue other legally available remedies [1826](#cite:1826). Under 200.342, on initiating a remedy the agency must give the recipient an opportunity to object and to provide information challenging the action [1828](#cite:1828). Under 200.343 costs from obligations incurred during a suspension or after termination are [unallowable](#term:allowable-cost) unless expressly authorised, except obligations properly incurred before the effective date and not in anticipation of it [1829](#cite:1829). The eCFR's version record for part 200, read on 2026-10-04, gives October 1, 2024 as the latest amendment date of the part; the only later issues are of 200.1, 200.405, Appendix VII and Appendix XII, each marked not substantive [2103](#cite:2103).
applies_to: Recipients and [subrecipients](#term:subrecipient) under Part 200 [1826](#cite:1826).

OMB's [proposed rule](#term:proposed-rule) would revise 200.340 to 200.343 to clarify agencies' ability to terminate discretionary awards for discretionary reasons consistent with law [1803](#cite:1803). An association summary says the proposal lists five grounds, including federal agency discretion [1878](#cite:1878). Section 157 of Public Law 119-103 bars a [final rule](#term:final-rule) through December 11, 2026 [1480](#cite:1480).

Read in the [Federal Register](#term:federal-register) text of OMB's proposal: proposed 200.340(a) lists five grounds, numbered (1) noncompliance by the recipient or [subrecipient](#term:subrecipient), (2) a determination by the agency or [pass-through entity](#term:pass-through-entity), to the extent permitted by law, that termination is in its interest, including where the award no longer effectuates programme goals, agency priorities or the national interest as they exist at the time of termination, (3) mutual agreement, (4) notification by the recipient or subrecipient and (5) additional termination provisions in the award; a new paragraph (d) would allow a written order to stop work [2093](#cite:2093) [2104](#cite:2104). Section 157 of Public Law 119-103 keeps a rule arising from the proposal from being issued or taking effect through December 11, 2026 [1480](#cite:1480).

name: Termination of an award (2 CFR 200.340)
what: Termination is the action an agency or pass-through entity takes to end an award, in whole or in part, before the planned end of the [period of performance](#term:budget-period) [1799](#cite:1799). 2 CFR 200.340 lists four ways an award may be terminated and requires every termination provision to be stated in the award terms [1801](#cite:1801). The fourth ground, for an award that "no longer effectuates the program goals or agency priorities", is the ground that [NSF](#term:nsf)'s public statements and [NIH](#term:nih)'s award terms use for priority-based terminations, and it is the subject of a July 2026 court ruling [1801](#cite:1801) [154](#cite:154) [65](#cite:65) [1869](#cite:1869).
rule: Under 2 CFR 200.340(a) an award may be terminated: (1) by the agency or pass-through entity if the recipient fails to comply with the terms and conditions; (2) by the agency or pass-through entity with the recipient's consent, on agreed conditions; (3) by the recipient, on written notice giving the reasons and effective date; or (4) by the agency or pass-through entity pursuant to the terms and conditions of the award, including, to the extent authorised by law, if an award no longer effectuates the programme goals or agency priorities [1801](#cite:1801). Under 200.340(b) the agency or pass-through entity must clearly and unambiguously specify all termination provisions in the award terms [1801](#cite:1801). Under 200.341 the agency must give written notice, which is to state the reasons, the effective date and the portion terminated [1827](#cite:1827). Where termination is for material failure to comply, the agency reports it in [SAM.gov](#term:sam-gov), where it stays available for five years, and the recipient may post comments there [1801](#cite:1801) [1827](#cite:1827). Under 200.343 costs after termination are allowable only if they result from obligations properly incurred before the effective date and not in anticipation of it, or are expressly authorised [1829](#cite:1829). After termination both sides remain responsible for [closeout](#term:closeout) [1801](#cite:1801). The District of Massachusetts declared on July 17, 2026 that 200.340(a)(4), and its 2021 predecessor 200.340(a)(2), do not allow termination based on new programme goals or agency priorities identified after the award was made [1869](#cite:1869). A second reading of 200.340 on the [eCFR](#term:cfr) on 2026-10-04, in the text current to 10/01/2026, returned the same four grounds; paragraph (c) has a termination for material noncompliance reported in SAM.gov only after the recipient has exhausted its opportunities to object or 30 calendar days have passed without notice of an appeal [1801](#cite:1801).

name: Challenging a termination: objections, agency appeals and the courts
what: A recipient whose award is terminated has two kinds of recourse: the procedures of the agency itself, and a suit in federal court [1828](#cite:1828) [28](#cite:28). Agency procedures differ by agency and by the reason given for the termination [1888](#cite:1888) [154](#cite:154). For a court challenge the question since 2025 has been which court: the Supreme Court has twice indicated that a claim to be paid under a terminated [grant](#term:grant) belongs in the Court of Federal Claims, while a challenge to an agency-wide policy may be heard in a district court [1804](#cite:1804) [28](#cite:28).
rule: Agency procedures: [2 CFR 200](#term:uniform-guidance).342 requires each federal agency to keep written procedures for objections, hearings and appeals; on initiating a remedy for noncompliance the agency must give the recipient an opportunity to object and to provide information challenging the action, and must follow any hearing or appeal a statute or regulation provides [1828](#cite:1828). At [HHS](#term:hhs) the Departmental Appeals Board hears, among [discretionary grant](#term:discretionary-grant) disputes, a termination for failure to comply with the terms of an award, a disallowance, a denial of a [noncompeting continuation](#term:continuation) for failure to comply, and a voiding, with a 30-day period for the notice of appeal [1888](#cite:1888). [NSF](#term:nsf) states that terminations on the ground that an award no longer effectuates programme goals or agency priorities are the final agency decision and are not appealable to NSF [154](#cite:154). Supreme Court: In Department of Education v. California (April 4, 2025) the Court stayed a district court order that had required continued payment of terminated teacher-training grants, stating that the APA's waiver of sovereign immunity does not extend to orders to enforce a contractual obligation to pay money and that the Tucker Act gives the Court of Federal Claims jurisdiction over suits based on a contract with the United States [1804](#cite:1804). In [National Institutes of Health](#term:nih) v. American Public Health Association (August 21, 2025) the Court stayed the district court judgments that [vacated](#term:vacatur) NIH grant terminations and declined to stay the judgments that vacated the NIH guidance documents; Justice Barrett, whose vote decided each part, wrote that the challenge to the guidance belongs in district court and the challenges to the terminations belong in the Court of Federal Claims [28](#cite:28). Both are orders on stay applications, not final rulings on the merits [1804](#cite:1804) [28](#cite:28). Courts of appeals in 2026: The Fourth Circuit (The Sustainability Institute v. Trump, January 21, 2026) vacated [injunctions](#term:injunction) restoring 32 grants, holding that the district court lacked jurisdiction to order relief designed to enforce obligations to pay money under the grants and that the plaintiffs' constitutional claims were statutory claims [1879](#cite:1879). The First Circuit (Massachusetts v. NIH, January 5, 2026) kept a challenge to NIH's agency-wide [indirect cost](#term:indirect-costs) policy in district court and affirmed its vacatur [24](#cite:24). The Ninth Circuit (Thakur v. Trump, May 26, 2026) reversed a class injunction for researchers whose grants were ended by form letter, as an APA claim that is in essence a contract action, and affirmed the injunction for the class whose grants were ended under the DEI [executive orders](#term:executive-order), on a First Amendment claim the Tucker Act does not bar [1867](#cite:1867). District court: In New Jersey v. OMB (July 17, 2026) the District of Massachusetts held that a claim about future terminations under the regulation was properly before it and that challenges to past terminations belong in the Court of Federal Claims [1869](#cite:1869). Court of Federal Claims: The opinions describe that court as able to award money damages for breach and not to reinstate a grant; the Ninth Circuit concurrence notes that a researcher who is not a party to the grant agreement faces a separate obstacle there [28](#cite:28) [1867](#cite:1867). The Federal Circuit held on February 4, 2026 that a grant statute with mandatory "shall award" language was money-mandating under the Tucker Act, in a case about the Restaurant Revitalization Fund [1868](#cite:1868).

name: Single audit (2 CFR part 200, subpart F)
what: A [single audit](#term:single-audit) is the audit a non-federal entity must have for any fiscal year in which its spending of federal awards reaches a set amount [1845](#cite:1845). The threshold in force is $1,000,000 in federal awards expended in the entity's fiscal year [1845](#cite:1845). The audit is filed with the [Federal Audit Clearinghouse](#term:federal-audit-clearinghouse), which GSA runs [1846](#cite:1846) [1881](#cite:1881).
rule: Under [2 CFR 200](#term:uniform-guidance).501(a) and (b) a non-federal entity that expends $1,000,000 or more in federal awards during its fiscal year must have a single audit, or a programme-specific audit where it qualifies, for that year [1845]. Under 200.501(e) an entity that expends less than $1,000,000 is exempt from federal audit requirements for that year, except as 200.503 provides [1845](#cite:1845). A programme-specific audit may be elected where the entity spends under only one federal programme, excluding research and development, and no financial statement audit is required [1845](#cite:1845). Money received as a [subrecipient](#term:subrecipient) counts as federal awards expended; payments received as a contractor do not [1845](#cite:1845). Under 200.512 the audit, data collection form and reporting package are submitted electronically to the Federal Audit Clearinghouse within 30 calendar days after the auditee receives the auditor's report or nine months after the end of the audit period, whichever is earlier [1846](#cite:1846). A [pass-through entity](#term:pass-through-entity) must verify that each subrecipient is audited when the rule requires [1823](#cite:1823). An auditee that meets the conditions in 200.520 for two audit periods is a low-risk auditee with reduced audit coverage [1847](#cite:1847). Audit reports and findings are among the factors in an agency's [pre-award risk review](#term:risk-review) [1809](#cite:1809). The [eCFR](#term:cfr) text of 200.501 current to 10/01/2026 carries the same $1,000,000 threshold, and the same exemption below it, with the source note 89 FR 30136, April 22, 2024 [1940](#cite:1940). The eCFR's version record for part 200 lists no issue of 200.512 or 200.520 after the amendment dated October 1, 2024 [2103](#cite:2103). The eCFR text of 200.512 current to 10/01/2026 has the same filing deadline [1939](#cite:1939).

name: Certifications on reports, payment requests and rate proposals (2 CFR 200.415)
what: The [Uniform Guidance](#term:uniform-guidance) itself requires an authorised official to sign a certification on each financial report and payment request [1885](#cite:1885). The certification names the federal false-statement and false-claims statutes, so the tie between [grant](#term:grant) paperwork and the False Claims Act predates the certifications added in 2025 [1885](#cite:1885).
rule: Under 2 CFR 200.415(a) the official certifies that the report is true, complete and accurate and that the expenditures, disbursements and cash receipts are for the purposes set out in the award, and acknowledges that false, fictitious or fraudulent information may bring criminal, civil or administrative penalties under 18 U.S.C. 1001 and 31 U.S.C. 3729-3730 and 3801-3812 [1885](#cite:1885). Under 200.415(b) a [subrecipient](#term:subrecipient) makes a parallel certification to the [pass-through entity](#term:pass-through-entity) when it applies for funds, requests payment and reports [1885](#cite:1885). Under 200.415(c) an [indirect cost](#term:indirect-costs) rate proposal is certified by an official no lower than vice president or chief financial officer; without it the agency may disallow indirect costs or set a rate itself [1885](#cite:1885). The [eCFR](#term:cfr)'s version record for part 200, read on 2026-10-04, gives October 1, 2024 as the latest amendment date of the part; the only later issues are of 200.1, 200.405, Appendix VII and Appendix XII, each marked not substantive [2103](#cite:2103).
applies_to: Recipients and subrecipients of awards under Part 200 [1885](#cite:1885).

name: Indirect (facilities and administrative) costs
what: [Indirect costs](#term:indirect-costs) are costs incurred for a common or joint purpose that benefit more than one cost objective and cannot readily be assigned to the award that benefits [1799](#cite:1799). For major [institutions of higher education](#term:institution-of-higher-education) and major non-profits they are classified in two groups, Facilities and Administration, which is why they are also called F&A costs [1802](#cite:1802). An award pays them as a percentage, the indirect cost rate, applied to a base of [direct costs](#term:direct-costs) [1849](#cite:1849) [1850](#cite:1850).
rule: For institutions of higher education Appendix III lists the F&A categories: depreciation, interest, operation and maintenance, general administration and general expenses, departmental administration, sponsored projects administration, library, and student administration and services [1849](#cite:1849). Appendix III, section C.8, limits the administrative categories at a university to 26% of [modified total direct costs](#term:mtdc) [1849](#cite:1849). For non-profits Appendix IV sets three allocation methods (simplified, multiple allocation base, direct allocation) and requires an organisation that receives more than $10 million in direct federal funding in a fiscal year to break its rate into Facilities and Administration [1850]. The base is normally modified total direct costs: salaries and wages, fringe benefits, materials and supplies, services, travel and up to the first $50,000 of each [subaward](#term:subaward), leaving out equipment, capital expenditures, patient care charges, rental costs, tuition remission, scholarships and fellowships, [participant support costs](#term:participant-support-costs) and the part of each subaward above $50,000 [1799](#cite:1799). An organisation gets its rate in one of two ways: a [negotiated indirect cost rate agreement](#term:nicra) with its [cognizant federal agency](#term:cognizant-agency), or the [de minimis rate](#term:de-minimis-rate) [1802](#cite:1802). The rate used for an award is printed in the award document [1810](#cite:1810). A cost may not be charged as direct if the same kind of cost in like circumstances is treated as indirect [1831](#cite:1831).

name: Modified total direct costs (MTDC)
what: [Modified total direct costs](#term:mtdc) are the base to which an [indirect cost](#term:indirect-costs) rate is usually applied [1799](#cite:1799). The definition decides which [direct costs](#term:direct-costs) carry indirect costs and which do not [1799](#cite:1799).
rule: [2 CFR 200](#term:uniform-guidance).1 defines MTDC as all direct salaries and wages, applicable fringe benefits, materials and supplies, services, travel, and up to the first $50,000 of each subaward, regardless of the period of performance of the subawards under the award [1799]. MTDC excludes equipment, capital expenditures, charges for patient care, rental costs, tuition remission, scholarships and fellowships, participant support costs, and the portion of each subaward in excess of $50,000 [1799](#cite:1799). Equipment for this purpose is property with a useful life of more than one year and a unit cost at or above the lesser of the organisation's capitalisation level or $10,000 [1799]. The $50,000 and $10,000 figures date from the revision effective October 1, 2024; a negotiated rate agreed before a revision stays in place until it expires and the revised definitions apply when the rate is renegotiated [1883] [1806]. A second reading of 200.1 on the eCFR on 2026-10-04, in the text current to 10/01/2026, returned the same $50,000 [subaward](#term:subaward) figure and the same $10,000 equipment figure [2102](#cite:2102).

name: Negotiated indirect cost rate agreement (NICRA)
what: A [negotiated indirect cost rate agreement](#term:nicra) records the rate, or rates, that one federal agency has negotiated with an organisation on behalf of all federal agencies [1799](#cite:1799). The agency that negotiates is the organisation's [cognizant agency for indirect costs](#term:cognizant-agency) [1799](#cite:1799). Once a rate is negotiated every federal agency must accept it, with the exceptions in negotiated-rate-acceptance-rule [1802](#cite:1802).
rule: Who negotiates: For an [institution of higher education](#term:institution-of-higher-education) the cognizant agency is [HHS](#term:hhs) or the Department of Defense's Office of Naval Research, normally whichever of the two provided more funds directly to the institution over the most recent three years, and the assignment lasts five years [1849](#cite:1849). For a non-profit it is the federal agency with the largest dollar value of awards made directly to the organisation [1850](#cite:1850). HHS negotiates through Cost Allocation Services, which handles colleges and universities, non-profits, hospitals and state and local governments; ONR negotiates for the domestic universities and non-profits for which it has cognizance; [NSF](#term:nsf)'s Cost Analysis and Pre-Award Branch negotiates for about 100 organisations [1860](#cite:1860) [1861](#cite:1861) [163](#cite:163). What is submitted and when: A non-profit with no established rate submits its first [indirect cost](#term:indirect-costs) proposal immediately after it is told an award will be made and no later than three months after the effective date of the award; an organisation with an established rate submits a new proposal within six months after the close of each fiscal year [1850](#cite:1850). Universities use the standard format in Appendix III, and those with no more than $10 million a year in covered [direct costs](#term:direct-costs) may use a simplified method [1849](#cite:1849). HHS takes all proposals through its Indirect Cost Allocation System portal [1860](#cite:1860). The proposal is certified by an official no lower than vice president or chief financial officer [1885](#cite:1885). How long a rate lasts: The appendices define predetermined, fixed, provisional and final rates; a predetermined rate at a university may cover two to four years [1849](#cite:1849) [1850](#cite:1850). An organisation with a current negotiated rate may ask once for an extension of up to four years, subject to the cognizant agency's approval, and must then renegotiate [1802](#cite:1802). For a university award, the rates in effect at the time of the initial award apply for the life of each [competitive segment](#term:budget-period) [1849](#cite:1849).

name: Rule that agencies must accept a negotiated rate, and its exceptions
what: A [negotiated indirect cost rate](#term:nicra) binds every federal agency, not only the one that negotiated it [1802](#cite:1802). The rule has two exceptions: a statute or regulation that requires a different rate, and a deviation the awarding agency approves under a published procedure [1802](#cite:1802). The courts that [set aside](#term:vacatur) the 2025 [rate caps](#term:indirect-rate-cap) relied on this rule [1854](#cite:1854) [1853](#cite:1853) [1855](#cite:1855).
rule: Under 2 CFR 200.414(c)(1) negotiated indirect cost rates must be accepted by all federal agencies; an agency may use a different rate for a class of awards or a single award only when a federal statute or regulation requires it or when the awarding agency approves it under paragraph (c)(3) [1802](#cite:1802). The agency must notify OMB of any approved deviation, must make public the policies, procedures and decision criteria it follows for deviations, and must state its indirect cost policies in the [notice of funding opportunity](#term:nofo) [1802](#cite:1802). Under 200.414(d) a [pass-through entity](#term:pass-through-entity) must accept a [subrecipient](#term:subrecipient)'s federally negotiated rate [1802](#cite:1802). For universities, Appendix III requires agencies to use the negotiated rates in effect at the time of the initial award throughout each [competitive segment](#term:budget-period) [1849](#cite:1849). Limits set by statute or regulation: [HHS](#term:hhs) regulations limit indirect costs on [training grants](#term:t32) to 8% of [modified total direct costs](#term:mtdc) and allow foreign organisations an 8% rate [1884](#cite:1884) [528](#cite:528). [Appropriations](#term:appropriations-act) provisions: Section 224 of the Labor-HHS division of Public Law 119-75 keeps the indirect cost provisions of 45 [CFR](#term:cfr) part 75, including approval of deviations from negotiated rates, applying to [NIH](#term:nih) as in the third quarter of fiscal year 2017 and bars spending to develop or implement a modified approach [1856](#cite:1856). DOE describes section 313 of the fiscal year 2026 Energy and Water act as requiring it to apply 2 CFR 200.414, including approval of deviations, as in fiscal year 2024 [289](#cite:289). Public Law 119-103 continues the fiscal year 2026 acts under their authority and conditions through December 11, 2026 [1480](#cite:1480). A second reading of 200.414(c) on the eCFR on 2026-10-04 returned the same rule that negotiated rates must be accepted by all Federal agencies [1802](#cite:1802). Part IX of the preamble to OMB's proposed rule states that OMB is not proposing updates to the indirect cost rate negotiation system through that document and may consider a request for information later [2093](#cite:2093).

NSF and DOE state that they apply negotiated rates, an appropriations provision keeps the earlier rules in place at NIH, and the Department of Defense policy is vacated and [enjoined](#term:injunction) [154](#cite:154) [289](#cite:289) [1856](#cite:1856) [1855](#cite:1855).

name: Executive Order 14332, Improving Oversight of Federal Grantmaking (August 7, 2025)
what: [Executive Order 14332](#term:executive-order-14332) changes how federal agencies decide on and manage [discretionary grants](#term:discretionary-grant) [246](#cite:246). It puts a senior appointee's review ahead of every new funding announcement and discretionary award, sets principles those awards are to follow, and directs changes to the Uniform Guidance and to award terms on [termination](#term:termination), [indirect costs](#term:indirect-costs) and drawdowns [246](#cite:246). It was signed August 7, 2025 and published at 90 FR 38929 [246](#cite:246).
rule: Scope: The order applies to discretionary grants, which it defines by reference to "discretionary award" in 2 CFR 200.1; one fetch of the order returned that the term excludes entitlement, formula-based and disaster recovery awards [246](#cite:246). Section 3: each agency head designates a senior appointee to review new funding opportunity announcements and discretionary grants for consistency with agency priorities and the national interest; the process includes subject-matter expert review for scientific research, pre-issuance review, interagency coordination, and a yearly review of discretionary awards [246](#cite:246). Section 4: senior appointees use independent judgment and do not ministerially ratify or routinely defer to what others propose; awards are to demonstrably advance the President's policy priorities; listed uses of funds are excluded; and, all else being equal, preference goes to institutions with lower indirect cost rates [246](#cite:246). Section 5: the [OMB](#term:omb) Director revises the Uniform Guidance to streamline application requirements, to clarify that discretionary grants permit termination for convenience, with listed exceptions, and to limit the use of discretionary grant funds for facilities and administrative costs [246](#cite:246). Section 6: within 30 days each agency head reviews the agency's standard [grant](#term:grant) terms and reports to OMB; agencies revise the terms of existing discretionary grants to permit immediate termination for convenience and add terms requiring written explanation for each drawdown [246](#cite:246). Section 7: the order creates no enforceable rights and is to be implemented consistent with applicable law [246](#cite:246). Implementation read in this sweep: DOE issued procedures for review of funding announcements on February 19, 2026 (Policy Flash 2026-33), with review of discretionary awards left to a later directive [314](#cite:314). [NIH](#term:nih)'s award terms from October 1, 2025 state the priority-based termination ground [65](#cite:65). OMB's [proposed rule](#term:proposed-rule) of May 29, 2026 is the revision of the Uniform Guidance that section 5 calls for; it has not been finalised and section 157 of Public Law 119-103 bars a [final rule](#term:final-rule) through December 11, 2026 [1803](#cite:1803) [1480](#cite:1480). The Uniform Guidance in force still requires agencies to accept negotiated indirect cost rates and limits termination to the four grounds in 200.340 [1802](#cite:1802) [1801](#cite:1801).

name: Anti-discrimination certification tied to the False Claims Act (2025-26)
what: [Executive Order](#term:executive-order) 14173 of January 21, 2025 directs every agency to put two terms in each [grant](#term:grant) award: an agreement that the recipient's compliance with federal anti-discrimination laws is material to the Government's payment decisions for purposes of the False Claims Act, and a certification that the recipient does not operate any programmes promoting DEI that violate those laws [1862](#cite:1862). A false certification can therefore be pursued as a false claim, by the Government or by a private party suing on its behalf [1863](#cite:1863). Agencies have carried the term into their own award conditions in different words and at different times [1870](#cite:1870) [528](#cite:528).
rule: The order: Section 3(b)(iv)(A) requires a term that compliance "in all respects with all applicable Federal anti-discrimination laws" is material for purposes of 31 U.S.C. 3729(b)(4); section 3(b)(iv)(B) requires the certification [1862](#cite:1862). Enforcement: A Deputy Attorney General memorandum of May 19, 2025 set up the Civil Rights Fraud Initiative, led by the Civil Division's Fraud Section and the Civil Rights Division, to use the False Claims Act where a recipient of federal funds knowingly violates civil rights laws and falsely certifies compliance, and encouraged private suits under 31 U.S.C. 3730 [1863](#cite:1863). An Attorney General memorandum of July 29, 2025 to all agencies lists five kinds of practice the department treats as unlawful and adds a list of practices it describes as non-binding suggestions [1864](#cite:1864). Agency terms: [NIH](#term:nih) added a civil rights term on April 21, 2025 (certification that the recipient does not operate programmes that advance or promote DEI, DEIA or discriminatory equity ideology in violation of federal anti-discrimination laws, and does not engage in a discriminatory prohibited boycott) and [rescinded](#term:rescission) it on June 12, 2025, saying it awaited federal-wide guidance [1870](#cite:1870) [1871](#cite:1871). The [HHS](#term:hhs) Grants Policy Statement effective October 1, 2025 states that by applying for or accepting HHS funds a recipient certifies compliance with all federal antidiscrimination laws, and that a knowing false statement may bring False Claims Act liability [528](#cite:528). SAM.gov: On January 28, 2026 GSA proposed to revise the financial assistance representations and certifications that every prime recipient makes when it registers or renews in SAM.gov, citing the Attorney General's guidance and Executive Order 14173; comments closed March 30, 2026, and no later notice was found [1866](#cite:1866). Existing rules: [2 CFR 200](#term:uniform-guidance).300 already requires awards to be administered in accordance with statutes prohibiting discrimination, and 200.415 already ties signed certifications on reports to the False Claims Act [1887](#cite:1887) [1885](#cite:1885). Court rulings: The District of Maryland enjoined the certification provision nationwide; the Fourth Circuit vacated that injunction on February 6, 2026, holding the plaintiffs unlikely to succeed on a facial First Amendment challenge because the provision requires certification of compliance with existing law, and noting that a recipient may contest an interpretation of that law in a specific enforcement action [1865](#cite:1865).
