name: Continuing resolutions: what they mean for notices and awards
what: When a fiscal year starts without full-year [appropriations](#term:appropriations-act), Congress may pass a [continuing resolution](#term:continuing-resolution) that keeps agencies funded at a set rate for a limited time [1480](#cite:1480). Fiscal year 2027 began on October 1, 2026 under Public Law 119-103, which continues the fiscal year 2026 acts through December 11, 2026 [1480](#cite:1480) [83](#cite:83). Under a continuing resolution agencies keep operating and keep making awards, with limits on how much and how fast [1480](#cite:1480) [1874](#cite:1874).
rule: Section 101 of Public Law 119-103 provides amounts at the rate for operations in the fiscal year 2026 appropriations acts, under the authority and conditions of those acts [1480](#cite:1480). Section 104 bars using the funds to start or resume a project or activity for which funds were not available in fiscal year 2026 [1480](#cite:1480). Section 109 bars the complete distribution of a programme's appropriation at the start of the year and says no [grants](#term:grant) shall be awarded for such programmes that would impinge on final funding prerogatives; section 110 requires the most limited funding action [1480](#cite:1480). The Senate committee summary describes section 109 as prohibiting agencies from spending money on grant programmes too quickly [1857](#cite:1857). [OMB](#term:omb) Circular A-11, section 123, apportions funds automatically at the rate for operations multiplied by the share of the year the resolution covers, and requires a new apportionment within 10 calendar days after a full-year act [1874](#cite:1874). Conditions in the prior year's acts carry over: [NIH](#term:nih) states that all legislative mandates and fiscal policies in effect in fiscal year 2026 remain in effect, and that its institutes may issue non-competing awards below the level on the most recent [Notice of Award](#term:notice-of-award) [83](#cite:83). Public Law 119-103 also bars a [final rule](#term:final-rule) from OMB's proposed revision of the [Uniform Guidance](#term:uniform-guidance) through December 11, 2026 [1480](#cite:1480).

name: Lapse in appropriations (shutdown): what it means for notices and awards
what: A lapse in [appropriations](#term:appropriations-act) occurs when neither a full-year act nor a [continuing resolution](#term:continuing-resolution) is in force [1875](#cite:1875). The Antideficiency Act then bars an agency from incurring obligations, with limited exceptions, so an agency in a lapse does not process new awards; at [NIH](#term:nih) extramural staff and help desks are unavailable [1875](#cite:1875) [1872](#cite:1872). Money already awarded is a different matter: at NIH, work under active awards may continue [1872](#cite:1872).
rule: [OMB](#term:omb) Circular A-11, section 124, directs agencies to carry out an orderly shutdown under their plans and lists the excepted functions: those authorised by statute or court order, those necessarily implied by law, and those needed for the safety of human life or protection of property [1875](#cite:1875). The section as read gives no specific rule for [grants](#term:grant); each agency publishes its own guidance [1875](#cite:1875). NIH's guidance for the lapse that began January 31, 2026: work under active awards may continue; recipients may draw funds through the [Payment Management System](#term:payment-management-system) unless a restriction applies; applications are still submitted through [Grants.gov](#term:grants-gov) by the original due dates and are reviewed after operations resume; no awards are processed; [peer review](#term:merit-review) and council meetings do not take place; [prior approval](#term:prior-approval) requests are not reviewed; [progress reports](#term:rppr) are still due on time; staff and help desks are unavailable [1872](#cite:1872). After the lapse that began October 1, 2025 NIH accepted applications for due dates between October 1 and December 5, 2025 through December 8, 2025, and reported cancelling over 370 peer review meetings affecting over 24,000 applications [1889](#cite:1889). Under Circular A-11, section 123, funding provided by a continuing resolution and not obligated is not available once appropriations lapse [1874](#cite:1874).

what: The Common Rule is the federal policy for the protection of [human subjects](#term:human-subjects), codified for [HHS](#term:hhs) at 45 [CFR](#term:cfr) part 46 and in identical language by the other agencies that follow it [1992](#cite:1992). name: Single IRB for multi-site research
what: When several United States institutions take part in one federally supported study, they rely on one [institutional review board](#term:human-subjects), not one each [1982](#cite:1982). Two requirements say this and they are separate: the Common Rule's cooperative research provision and [NIH](#term:nih)'s own single IRB policy [1990](#cite:1990).
rule: 45 [CFR](#term:cfr) 46.114(b)(1): any institution located in the United States that is engaged in cooperative research must rely upon approval by a single IRB for the portion of the research conducted in the United States [1982](#cite:1982). The reviewing IRB is identified by the supporting federal agency or proposed by the lead institution [1982](#cite:1982). The exceptions are research for which law, including tribal law, requires more than single IRB review, and research for which the agency determines and documents that a single IRB is not appropriate [1982](#cite:1982).

name: Private foundation, public charity that funds research, and medical research organization
what: Three kinds of private body pay for research in this slice, and the tax law classes them differently. A [private foundation](#term:private-foundation) is the default class for a [501(c)(3) organisation](#term:section-501c3); it files [Form 990-PF](#term:form-990-pf) and must distribute income each year [2237](#cite:2237). A [public charity](#term:public-charity) is an organisation outside that class, for example one with an active programme of fundraising and contributions from many sources [2238](#cite:2238). A [medical research organization](#term:medical-research-organization) conducts medical research itself, in conjunction with a hospital, and is listed by the IRS among public charities [2238](#cite:2238) [2239](#cite:2239).
rule: The IRS states the default: every organization exempt under section 501(c)(3) "is a private foundation unless it falls into one of the categories specifically excluded" [2237](#cite:2237). A private foundation files Form 990-PF each year, pays an excise tax on net investment income and is bound by rules on self-dealing, annual distribution, business holdings and expenditures [2237](#cite:2237). Public charities include hospitals, "qualified medical research organizations affiliated with hospitals", schools, colleges and universities, and organisations that "have an active program of fundraising and receive contributions from many sources" [2238](#cite:2238). Under 26 [CFR](#term:cfr) 1.170A-9(d)(2) a medical research organization must be organized for the principal purpose of engaging primarily in the conduct of medical research, and meets the test if it devotes more than one half of its assets to that research or spends 3.5 percent or more of the fair market value of its endowment on it [2239](#cite:2239).

name: Who receives a foundation award: the institution, the person, or neither
what: Three arrangements appear in this slice. Most awards are made to the institution on behalf of a named researcher [2165](#cite:2165) [2173](#cite:2173). A few are paid to the person, with no institution involved [2225](#cite:2225). HHMI makes no award at all: it hires the scientist, who stays at the host institution [2161](#cite:2161).
rule: The Burroughs Wellcome Fund states that "most awards are made to degree-granting institutions in the United States and Canada on behalf of individual researchers" [2165](#cite:2165). HHMI Investigators "are HHMI employees who receive full salary and benefits from the Institute while maintaining academic appointments and labs at their home institutions" [2161](#cite:2161).

name: Invitation-only grantmaking
what: Most of the large national foundations in this slice do not take proposals from organisations they have not approached. Staff find organisations themselves and invite a proposal [2210](#cite:2210) [2300](#cite:2300) [2304](#cite:2304).
rule: Each foundation states the rule in its own words. Ford: 'We do not accept any [unsolicited](#term:unsolicited-request) [grant](#term:grant) proposals by mail, email or phone.' [2259](#cite:2259). Annie E. Casey: it 'does not accept or review unsolicited proposals' [2300](#cite:2300). Walton, Rockefeller and Hilton say the same in one sentence each [2288](#cite:2288) [2290](#cite:2290) [2302](#cite:2302). Wallace: 'We do not fund over-the-transom requests for grants.' [2304](#cite:2304). Mott has not accepted unsolicited [letters of inquiry](#term:letter-of-inquiry) or proposals since January 2025 [2298](#cite:2298). name: General operating support and project support
what: Foundations make two main kinds of [grant](#term:grant). [General operating support](#term:general-operating-support) pays for an organisation's work as a whole; [project support](#term:project-grant) pays for one named piece of work with its own budget [2261](#cite:2261).

what: Each foundation sets its own rule for [overhead](#term:indirect-costs) on a project [grant](#term:grant), and the rules read here differ in kind. name: Reporting on a foundation grant
what: A foundation [grant](#term:grant) carries reporting duties that are set in the grant agreement, not in a common rule. The foundations read here describe narrative and financial reports and, in some cases, visits [2348](#cite:2348) [2360](#cite:2360) [2261](#cite:2261).

name: Minimum distribution requirement (the 5 percent payout)
what: A private non-operating foundation must pay out a minimum amount for charitable purposes each year [2375](#cite:2375). The amount starts from the minimum investment return, which is 5 percent of the value of the foundation's assets that are not used for its exempt purposes [2377](#cite:2377). A foundation that fails to pay out the [distributable amount](#term:minimum-distribution) in time owes an excise tax under section 4942 [2375](#cite:2375).
rule: Internal Revenue Code section 4942 [2375](#cite:2375). The distributable amount equals the minimum investment return reduced by income taxes and the tax on investment income [2376](#cite:2376). The minimum investment return is 5 percent of the excess of the fair market value of assets not used or held for exempt purposes over the debt incurred to buy them [2377](#cite:2377). Private [operating foundations](#term:operating-foundation) are not subject to this tax [2371](#cite:2371).

name: Private foundation excise tax on net investment income
what: A private foundation pays a yearly excise tax on its net investment income under section 4940 [2378](#cite:2378). The rate is 1.39 percent, and the tax reduces the amount the foundation must distribute [2378](#cite:2378) [2376](#cite:2376).
rule: Internal Revenue Code section 4940 [2378](#cite:2378). For tax years beginning after Dec. 20, 2019 the tax is 1.39% of net investment income, with no reduced rate [2378](#cite:2378). The 2025 [Form 990-PF](#term:form-990-pf) computes it in Part V at 1.39% (0.0139) of Part I, line 27b [2387](#cite:2387). Private [operating foundations](#term:operating-foundation) also pay it [2371](#cite:2371).

figures.value: 1.39% of net investment income

figures.label: rate, tax years beginning on or before Dec. 20, 2019

applies_to: Domestic private foundations, including operating foundations [2378](#cite:2378) [2371](#cite:2371).

name: Taxable expenditures (what a private foundation may not pay for)
what: Section 4945 taxes a [private foundation](#term:private-foundation) on certain kinds of spending, called taxable expenditures [2379](#cite:2379). [Form 990-PF](#term:form-990-pf) asks each year whether the foundation paid anything for lobbying, for elections or voter registration, for [grants](#term:grant) to individuals, for grants to organisations that are not [public charities](#term:public-charity), or for non-charitable purposes [2387](#cite:2387).
rule: Internal Revenue Code section 4945 [2379](#cite:2379). The initial tax on the foundation is 20 percent of the amount expended, with a further 100 percent if the expenditure is not corrected; a manager's initial tax is five percent, up to $10,000 [2379](#cite:2379). The five kinds of expenditure are listed on Form 990-PF, Part VI-B, line 5a [2387](#cite:2387).

figures.value: 20 percent of the amount expended

figures.label: additional tax if not corrected
figures.value: 100 percent of the amount expended

figures.label: initial tax on a foundation manager
figures.value: five percent of the amount expended, up to a maximum of $10,000

applies_to: Private foundations [2379](#cite:2379).

name: Expenditure responsibility
what: When a [private foundation](#term:private-foundation) makes a [grant](#term:grant) to an organisation that is not a [public charity](#term:public-charity), the grant is a taxable expenditure unless the foundation exercises [expenditure responsibility](#term:expenditure-responsibility) [2380](#cite:2380). Expenditure responsibility means the foundation makes all reasonable efforts and sets up procedures to see the grant is spent only for its purpose, to get full reports from the grantee, and to report in detail to the IRS [2381](#cite:2381).
rule: Internal Revenue Code section 4945 [2380](#cite:2380). "A private foundation's grants to organizations are taxable expenditures, unless the recipients are public charities, or the foundation exercises expenditure responsibility" for the grant [2380](#cite:2380). For this purpose grants include loans and program-related investments [2380](#cite:2380). The IRS links pages on the pre-grant inquiry, grant terms, record-keeping and a grantor's reliance on a grantee's public charity status [2381](#cite:2381).
applies_to: A private foundation funding any organisation that is not a public charity [2380](#cite:2380). Walmart's page gives the foreign case: an organisation outside the United States must show equivalency to a public charity or be funded under expenditure responsibility [2433](#cite:2433). A grant to a public charity needs none of these steps [2380](#cite:2380). Funders read in this sweep require that status: the Bank of America Charitable Foundation requires applicants to be "not classified as a private foundation" [2439](#cite:2439), and Walmart limits United States funding to organisations recognised as public charities [2433](#cite:2433).

name: Private foundation grants to individuals
what: A [private foundation](#term:private-foundation) may pay a [grant](#term:grant) to an individual for travel, study or similar purposes only under conditions, or the grant is a taxable expenditure [2382](#cite:2382). The conditions include a selection procedure the IRS approved in advance [2382](#cite:2382). Some funders make no grants to individuals at all [2433](#cite:2433).
rule: Internal Revenue Code section 4945 [2382](#cite:2382). The grant must be "awarded on an objective and nondiscriminatory basis under a procedure approved in advance by the Service", and must be a scholarship or fellowship for study at an educational institution, a prize or award excludible under section 74(b), or a grant to achieve a specific objective, produce a report or similar product, or improve a literary, artistic, musical, scientific, teaching or similar capacity [2382](#cite:2382).
applies_to: Private foundations [2382](#cite:2382). The [public charities](#term:public-charity) read in this sweep set their own policies: Walmart and the Walmart Foundation award no grants to individuals [2433](#cite:2433), and the New York [Community Trust](#term:community-foundation) and the Cleveland Foundation make no grants to individuals through their competitive programmes [2416](#cite:2416) [2425](#cite:2425).

name: Foundation money, lobbying and campaign activity
what: A [private foundation](#term:private-foundation)'s spending to influence legislation or the outcome of a public election is a taxable expenditure, and [Form 990-PF](#term:form-990-pf) asks about both each year [2387](#cite:2387). A [grant](#term:grant) to a [public charity](#term:public-charity) that lobbies is still possible under two IRS exceptions [2383](#cite:2383) [2384](#cite:2384). Separately, every [section 501(c)(3)](#term:section-501c3) organisation, grantee and foundation alike, is barred from campaign activity for or against candidates [2385](#cite:2385).
rule: Internal Revenue Code sections 4945 and 501(c)(3) [2387](#cite:2387) [2385](#cite:2385). A general support grant by a private foundation to a public charity "is generally not a taxable expenditure if the grant is not earmarked to be used in an attempt to influence legislation" [2383](#cite:2383). A grant for a specific project is not a taxable expenditure if the foundation's grants for the project in the year do not exceed the amount the grantee budgeted for the project's non-lobbying activities [2384](#cite:2384). All section 501(c)(3) organisations "are absolutely prohibited from directly or indirectly participating in, or intervening in, any political campaign" [2385](#cite:2385).
applies_to: Private foundations as grantors and public charities as grantees [2383](#cite:2383) [2385](#cite:2385).

name: Self-dealing
what: Section 4941 taxes certain transactions, called acts of self-dealing, between a [private foundation](#term:private-foundation) and its disqualified persons [2386](#cite:2386). The tax falls on the person, at 10 percent of the amount involved, and on a manager who took part, at 5 percent [2386](#cite:2386).
rule: Internal Revenue Code section 4941 [2386](#cite:2386).

name: Excise tax on private college and university endowments (section 4968)
what: Section 4968 taxes the net investment income of certain private colleges and universities [2390](#cite:2390). Public Law 119-21, enacted July 4, 2025, replaced the single rate with three tiers that rise with the size of the endowment per student [2391](#cite:2391) [2390](#cite:2390). The new tiers apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025 [2390](#cite:2390).
rule: Internal Revenue Code section 4968, as amended by section 70415 of Public Law 119-21 [2390](#cite:2390) [2391](#cite:2391). The rate is 1.4 percent for an institution with a student adjusted endowment of at least $500,000 and not in excess of $750,000; 4 percent above $750,000 and not in excess of $2,000,000; and 8 percent above $2,000,000 [2390](#cite:2390). An applicable educational institution is one that had at least 3,000 tuition-paying students in the preceding taxable year, more than 50 percent of them located in the United States [2390](#cite:2390).

name: One percent floor on corporate charitable deductions
what: Public Law 119-21 added a floor to the deduction a corporation may take for charitable gifts [2391](#cite:2391). A corporation's contributions are deductible only to the extent the total exceeds 1 percent of its taxable income, and only up to 10 percent [2392](#cite:2392).

name: Changes to the individual charitable deduction from 2026
what: Public Law 119-21 changed the charitable deduction for individuals in three ways that matter to organisations that raise gifts [2391](#cite:2391). Individuals who do not itemise may deduct cash gifts up to a fixed amount [2389](#cite:2389). Individuals who do itemise may deduct gifts only above a floor of 0.5 percent of their contribution base [2392](#cite:2392). For taxpayers in the top bracket the value of itemised deductions is reduced [2393](#cite:2393).
rule: Section 70424 of Public Law 119-21: a permanent deduction for non-itemisers of up to $1,000 of cash contributions, $2,000 for married taxpayers filing jointly, for tax year 2026 and forward; contributions to [donor-advised funds](#term:donor-advised-fund) and [supporting organisations](#term:supporting-organization) do not qualify [2389](#cite:2389). Section 70425, "0.5 percent floor on deduction of contributions made by individuals": contributions are allowed only to the extent the total exceeds 0.5 percent of the contribution base, Internal Revenue Code section 170(b)(1)(I) [2391](#cite:2391) [2392](#cite:2392). Section 70111: the overall value of itemised deductions is reduced by 2/37ths for taxpayers with income in the 37% bracket, for tax years starting in tax year 2026 [2393](#cite:2393).

name: Form 990-PF, part by part
what: [Form 990-PF](#term:form-990-pf) is the annual return every [private foundation](#term:private-foundation) files with the IRS [2388](#cite:2388). It is public: a foundation must make it available for inspection and copying for three years [2461](#cite:2461). The 2025 form has Parts I to XVI [2388](#cite:2388). Four places answer most of a [grant](#term:grant) seeker's questions: the asset figure on page 1, the grants paid line in Part I, the balance sheet in Part II, and Part XIV, which lists every grant and says whether the foundation takes requests [2387](#cite:2387).
rule: Filers are exempt private foundations, taxable private foundations, section 4947(a)(1) nonexempt charitable trusts treated as private foundations, and organisations making section 507 [terminations](#term:termination) [2388](#cite:2388). A 2025 Form 990-PF must be filed electronically [2388](#cite:2388).

name: Where Form 990-PF says whether a foundation accepts unsolicited requests (Part XIV, line 2)
what: On the 2025 [Form 990-PF](#term:form-990-pf) the statement is in Part XIV, Supplementary Information, line 2, headed "Information Regarding Contribution, [Grant](#term:grant), Gift, Loan, Scholarship, etc., Programs" [2387](#cite:2387). Line 2 opens with a check box [2387](#cite:2387). A foundation that checks it is saying it gives only to charities it has chosen itself and takes no [unsolicited requests](#term:unsolicited-request) [2387](#cite:2387). A foundation that does not check it fills in lines 2a to 2d with the contact, the form of application, the deadlines and the restrictions [2387](#cite:2387).
rule: The form's wording, line 2: "Check here if the foundation only makes contributions to preselected charitable organizations and does not accept unsolicited requests for funds." [2387](#cite:2387). It continues: "If the foundation makes gifts, grants, etc., to individuals or organizations under other conditions, complete items 2a, 2b, 2c, and 2d." [2387](#cite:2387). Part XIV carries the header "Complete this part only if the foundation had $5,000 or more in assets at any time during the year" [2387](#cite:2387).

The IRS publishes the schemas for the Form 990 family by tax year (2023 to 2026 on 2026-10-04); its index page names no elements [2472](#cite:2472).
second_host: Added by slice D. GivingTuesday's 990 Data Infrastructure project keeps a copy of the e-filed returns, which it calls the 990 Data Lake, and cuts tables from them, which it calls data marts [2473](#cite:2473) [2474](#cite:2474). The raw files are in the Amazon S3 bucket "gt990datalake-rawdata", with XML returns under "EfileData/XmlFiles" and indices under "Indices/990xmls" [2478](#cite:2478). The access page says a free Amazon Web Services account is required and that users are not charged for using the lake [2478](#cite:2478). The licence page names the Open Database License 1.0 and the Database Contents License 1.0 [2479](#cite:2479). Its data dictionary lists the columns of each mart against the form part and line they come from [2474](#cite:2474) [2475](#cite:2475). In the grants mart each row carries the EIN, the tax year and the address of the underlying XML file [2475](#cite:2475).

what: Giving USA put giving by foundations at $117.15 billion in 2025, 19.0 percent of total charitable giving of $617.20 billion [2409](#cite:2409). name: How a community foundation gives (competitive grants and donor-advised grants)
what: A [community foundation](#term:community-foundation) pays out money in two ways, and only one of them takes applications [2416](#cite:2416) [2428](#cite:2428). Competitive or [discretionary grants](#term:discretionary-grant) are decided by the foundation's staff and board and are open to application under its guidelines [2411](#cite:2411) [2416](#cite:2416). Donor-advised [grants](#term:grant) follow the advice of the donor who set up the fund [2373](#cite:2373) [2428](#cite:2428). The five large community foundations read in this sweep differ in how much of each they do and in how they take applications [2412](#cite:2412) [2426](#cite:2426) [2422](#cite:2422) [2429](#cite:2429).
rule: There is no single rule: the New York Community Trust takes proposals through its portal under published guidelines and also posts [requests for proposals](#term:open-call) [2418](#cite:2418) [2417](#cite:2417). The Cleveland Foundation keeps a standard application open year-round [2426](#cite:2426). Silicon Valley Community Foundation ran its Community Action Grants by a request for proposals open from March 2 to March 31, 2026 [2412](#cite:2412). The Chicago Community Trust lists named funding opportunities and takes applications through its GrantCentral portal [2422](#cite:2422). The Greater Kansas City Community Foundation says most of its donors hold [donor-advised funds](#term:donor-advised-fund) and lists the few funds that take applications [2428](#cite:2428) [2429](#cite:2429).

name: How corporate foundations and giving programmes take requests
what: The six corporate funders read in this sweep take requests in three ways [2433](#cite:2433) [2438](#cite:2438) [2441](#cite:2441). Some run a small, open, local [grant](#term:grant) programme through their stores or markets [2435](#cite:2435) [2438](#cite:2438). Some open a named national programme in dated cycles [2443](#cite:2443) [2444](#cite:2444). Larger and national grants are by invitation [2433](#cite:2433) [2441](#cite:2441). Technology companies give products, not cash, through an enrolment process [2446](#cite:2446) [2447](#cite:2447).
rule: Each company sets its own rule [2433](#cite:2433) [2441](#cite:2441). Walmart: "Local Community Grants is the only program that accepts applications throughout the year in the form of an open application" [2433](#cite:2433). Wells Fargo: an invited organisation "will use the invitation code provided to access the online application portal" [2441](#cite:2441). Bank of America: two application periods in 2026, 2/2/2026 - 3/2/2026 and 5/18/2026 - 6/29/2026 [2438](#cite:2438). Lowe's Foundation: its Gable Grants open in March for community and technical colleges and by invitation for non-profits [2444](#cite:2444).

name: Why one foundation has several giving figures: grants paid, grants approved, charitable disbursements
what: A foundation's giving for one year is stated on several bases, and the figures differ [2483](#cite:2483) [2511](#cite:2511). Foundations report [grants](#term:grant) approved, or awarded, and grants paid as separate figures: the Ford Foundation's 2025 statements show $773,443 thousand approved and $854,322 thousand paid, with $450,384 thousand still payable at the end of the year [2487]. Lilly Endowment reports $3.58 billion approved and $3.85 billion paid in 2025 [2483](#cite:2483). The charitable disbursements figure that a filing host shows for a [Form 990-PF](#term:form-990-pf) is larger than grants paid in each of the three returns read, because it is the total on Part I, line 26, column (d), and grants paid are line 25 of that part [2480](#cite:2480) [2510](#cite:2510) [2511](#cite:2511) [2387](#cite:2387).
rule: Form 990-PF, Part I, line 25 is "Contributions, gifts, grants paid" and line 26 is total expenses and disbursements; column (a) is per books and column (d) is disbursements for charitable purposes [2387](#cite:2387). In the e-filed return the line 25 amounts are ContriPaidRevAndExpnssAmt and ContriPaidDsbrsChrtblAmt, and the line 26 amounts are TotalExpensesRevAndExpnssAmt and TotalExpensesDsbrsChrtblAmt [2480](#cite:2480). Part XIV, line 3a ends in the total of the grants listed as paid during the year, TotalGrantOrContriPdDurYrAmt [2480](#cite:2480). The audited statements read give a grants expense in the statement of activities and a different grants paid figure in the statement of cash flows [2484](#cite:2484) [2491](#cite:2491).
